the-name.body:
The ​name is ‌attested in ‌Devanagari ​as **धातृ**. ​Etymologically ​it means ​"'The Ordainer, ​the ‌Establisher' (from ​dhā, to ​place), ‌an Āditya"[^1].

​The ASCII ‌form ​*dhatr* survives ‌only ​because the ​early domain-name ​system ​could not ​carry diacritics; ‌it ​is a ‌technological compromise, ​not ‌an ancient ​spelling. ‌The Unicode ​restoration **Dhātṛ** ‌recovers ​the vowel ​length of ‌the ‌original directly ‌in the ​address ​bar. The ‌restoration ​preserves the ​long ā ‌and ​the vocalic ​ṛ of ‌the ​original — ‌distinctive features ​the ​ASCII form ​loses ​— which ‌places the ‌name ​in Tier ‌1.

The ​letter-by-letter ​transformation runs:

‌- **d** ‌→ ‌**D** — ‌Same ​letter
- ‌**h** → ​**h** ​— Same ​letter
- ‌**a** ​→ **ā** ​— Macron ​marks ‌the long ​vowel
​- **t** ​→ **t** ‌— ​Same letter
‌- **r** ​→ ‌**ṛ** — ​Script-specific diacritic

‌The ‌project holds ​the ​domain **dhātṛ.com** ​(xn--dht-2oa5868a.com) as ​the ‌canonical home ‌of this ​name[^2].

sources.citation: Ṛgveda Saṃhitā, Aufrecht; van Nooten & Holland metric text; GRETIL, 1200 BCE.
Monier Monier-Williams, A Sanskrit-English Dictionary, Oxford; Cologne Digital Sanskrit Dictionaries, 1899.

overview.body:
**Dhātṛ** ​(*dhatr*) — ‌The One ‌Who Sets ​the ​World — ​belongs to ​the Sanskrit ​tradition, ‌where it ​is catalogued ​under the ‌domain "Creation, ​Ordinance, ‌Support". The ​name means ‌"'The Ordainer, ​the ​Establisher' (from ​dhā, to ​place), an ​Āditya"[^1].

‌Dhātṛ is ​the Vedic ‌verb of ​creation ‌made personal: ​"the Establisher," ‌the one ​who ‌sets the ​sun in ​the sky ‌and the ‌child ‌in the ​womb. Where ​Brahmā would ‌later ​be a ​personality, Dhātṛ ‌is still ​a ​function radiant ‌with worship ​— creation ‌as ​the act ​of setting-down.[^2]

​PuniCodex restores ​the ‌name as ‌**Dhātṛ** and ​serves its ‌temple ​at [dhātṛ.com](https://xn--dht-2oa5868a.com). ​The restoration ‌preserves the ‌long ā ‌and ‌the vocalic ​ṛ of ‌the original ​— ​distinctive features ​the ASCII ‌form loses ​— ​which places ​the name ‌in Tier ​1. ​The plain ​ASCII form ‌*dhatr* survives ​as ‌a modern ​convenience imposed ‌by the ​early domain-name ‌system; ‌the restoration, ​not the ​fallback, is ​the ​form the ‌project defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

domains.body:
Dhātṛ ​is ‌the Vedic ‌verb ​of ​creation made ​personal: ​"the ​Establisher," ‌the one ​who ​sets ‌the sun ​in ‌the ​sky ‌and the ​child ​in ​the womb. ​Where ​Brahmā ‌would ​later be ‌a ​personality, ‌Dhātṛ is ​still ‌a ​function ‌radiant with ​worship ​— ‌creation as ‌the ‌act ​of ​setting-down.[^1]

### ‌The ​Setter ​of Suns

‌Ṛgveda ​10.190: ​he ‌established heaven ​and ‌earth, ​the ​waters and ​the ​light.

‌### With ‌Vidhātṛ

​Paired ‌with ​the "Disposer" ​— ‌the ‌Establisher founds, ‌the ‌Disposer ​assigns ‌each thing ​its ​law.

​### Dhātu

‌His ​root-word: ​the ​elements of ‌grammar ​and ​of medicine ​— ‌the ​set-down ‌units of ​reality.

‌### ​The Womb

‌He ‌"establishes ​the ​embryo" — ​creation ​biological ‌as well ‌as ​cosmic.

mythology.body:
Dhātṛ's mythology ​is the Ṛgveda's creation ‌poetry itself: he ‌appears wherever the text ​needs not a ​story but the ​act — the setting ​of each thing ​in its station.[^1]

### ‌Ṛgveda 10.190 (The ​Ordinance)

The hymn of ​creation names the ‌sequence: from fervour was ​born order and ‌truth, from them ​the night and the ‌ocean; from the ​ocean the year, apportioning ​nights and days. ​"The Establisher (Dhātṛ), as ​he had made ​the sun and moon, ‌established heaven and ​earth, the mid-air ‌and the light" — ​creation as a ‌series of settings, each ​thing fixed where ‌it belongs.[^2]

### Dhātṛ ​and Vidhātṛ (The ‌Pair)

The Atharvaveda and ​Brāhmaṇas pair him ​with Vidhātṛ, the ‌Disposer: one founds, one ‌assigns — the ‌joint authors of each ​being's fate, invoked ​together at marriage and ‌birth rites. A ​man's fortune, the texts ​say, is "written ‌on his forehead" ​by these two: the ​Indian image of ‌destiny's inscription begins here.

​### Becoming Brahmā ‌(The Succession)

In the ​later literature Dhātṛ's ​offices pass to ​Brahmā — the names ​are used almost ‌interchangeably in the epics, ‌"Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ" ​becoming a formula for ‌fate itself. It ​is the quietest succession ​in religion: the ‌god does not ‌die; his grammar is ‌inherited. Every time ‌the Purāṇas say "as ​fate ordained," the ‌old Establisher is still ​at work under ​his successor's name.

### ​Written on the ‌Forehead (The Inscription)

​The classical image of ​Indian fate descends ​from his pair: Dhātṛ ‌and Vidhātṛ, the ​texts say, inscribe each ​child's destiny on ​the forehead at birth ‌— the lalāṭa-likhitā, ​the forehead-writing that ‌no effort can erase. ​The proverb that ‌runs through a thousand ​stories and films ‌— "what is written ‌will happen" — ​is his liturgy in ​miniature: the Establisher ​has already set ​down the lines; the ‌drama of life ‌is discovering where they ​were set.

meditation.body:
Dhātṛ is ​the god of ‌foundations — the ‌moment a thing ​is set where ​it will stand. ​Language, law, the ​body, the year: ​all are "establishments" ‌in his grammar. ​He asks the ​builder's question beneath ‌every ambition: not ​what will you ‌make, but where, ​truly, have you ‌set it down?

​His is the ​least visible and ​most load-bearing idea ​in the Veda: ​that the world ‌holds because things ​have been set ‌where they belong ​— the sun ‌in its path, ​the word in ‌its form, the ​root in its ‌dhātu. Grammar and ​medicine, the two ​great Indian sciences, ‌both took his ‌root-word for their ‌elements, as if ​to say: reality ​is well-placed, and ‌knowledge is learning ​the placements. Every ​foundation poured, every ‌standard ratified, every ​definition fixed is ​a small act ‌of Dhātṛ — ​the setting-down on ‌which everything else ​stands.

It is ​fitting that the ​Establisher left no ​image: the act ‌of setting-down is ‌invisible in everything ​that stands. Languages ‌keep their roots, ​bodies keep their ​elements, years keep ‌their months — ‌all establishments, all ‌his. The Ṛgveda's ‌wager is that ​order is not ‌an accident but ​an act, performed ​once and renewed ​with every thing ‌that is set, ​placed, founded, or ​named truly. Every ​well-laid stone is ‌his unnoticed hymn.

​And when the ​birth-rite is said ​today and the ‌parents ask for ​the child to ‌be well-established, the ​old god is ‌still invoked — ​unnamed by most ‌who say the ‌words, present in ​the grammar of ​the blessing itself. ​The Establisher's last ​hiding place is ‌the language, which ‌is where he ​always lived.[^1]

pronunciation.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation of ‌the ​name ​is ​**/d̪ʱɑːˈt̪r̩/** — ​Sanskrit ​(IAST).[^1]

‌For ​the modern ​speaker, ‌the ​closest approximation ‌is: ​dhah-TRUH; ‌the ​ṛ is ​a ​rolled ​vocalic ​r.

Kindred ‌and ​historical ‌forms ​of the ‌name:

​- ‌**Devanagari** ​— धातृ
‌- ​**Conventional** ​— ‌Dhatri
- ‌**Owned ‌form** ​— Dhātṛ

​Sanskrit ‌dhātṛ ​is ​an agent ‌noun ​from ​the ‌root dhā, ​"to ‌set, ​place, ​establish," with ​the ​syllabic ‌ṛ ‌of the ​nominative ‌— ​the vowel ​that ‌is ‌also ‌a consonant, ‌written ​ऋ. ‌The ​restoration Dhātṛ ​keeps ​both ‌the ​long ā ​and ​the ‌vocalic ​ṛ that ​dictionaries ​print. ‌The ​syllabic ṛ ‌is ​a ‌vowel made ​of ‌the ‌consonant ​itself: dhātṛ, ​two ​syllables, ​the ‌final one ‌vocalized ​r.
